questions.question: What does a hobby servo read from its signal wire to decide its angle?
questions.answer: The width of a pulse repeated about 50 times per second; roughly 0.5 ms is one end and 2.4 ms the other end of the range.
rubric: Short = one end, long = other end
questions.hint: It is not the voltage level.

questions.question: With a 500 to 2400 microsecond range for 0 to 180 degrees, roughly what pulse gives 90 degrees?
Why should five servos not be powered from the ESP32's 5V pin or the laptop USB port?
questions.answer: Servos draw large current, several amps together when moving or stalled; USB and the board regulator cannot supply that, so voltage dips and the board resets.

questions.question: The servo is powered from a 5 V supply and the signal wire is on GPIO13, but it jitters or does nothing. What wire may be missing?
questions.answer: A ground link between the supply and the ESP32 GND, so the signal has no common reference.
questions.hint: Both sides must measure from the same zero.

questions.question: What range of angles should you pass to myServo.write() in this course, and why not 0 and 180 or higher?
questions.answer: Keep angles between 10 and 170. The ends (0 and 180) are mechanical stops where the motor strains, and values above 180 are outside the servo's range.

questions.question: The servo hums and the hand body shakes when it reaches 180 degrees against the end stop. What do you change?
questions.answer: Limit the angle in code to a safe range such as 10 to 170 so the motor does not push against its stop.
questions.hint: Don't ask for more than the part can do.

questions.question: Explain in your own words why the capacitor across the servo power rail helps.
questions.answer: It stores a little charge and supplies sudden bursts of current when a servo starts, smoothing dips in the supply voltage.
